617.title: No requests today
617.hook: on Shabbat the weekday requests are replaced by one blessing of the day's holiness
617.carry: already enough, just as it is
617.howItsDone: The Shabbat Amidah has seven blessings: the first three and last three of the weekday Amidah, with the thirteen petitions replaced by one central blessing for the holiness of the day, worded differently at each Shabbat service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, l'hodot, Psalm 92's Sabbath song that never says Sabbath. Your line was good to give thanks. Who did you thank for something steady? Today, what Shabbat takes out of the prayer book. Day six hundred seventeen.

Help me understand this. Forgive me for that. Heal my friend. Help with money. Fix this mess. A normal week can run on requests. The weekday Amidah is built the same way. We walked through it earlier this year: a prayer of nineteen blessings, and the long middle is one request after another. Wisdom, forgiveness, healing, a good year's harvest, justice, peace. Then Friday night comes, you open the prayer book to the same place, and the middle is gone.
screen: `A WEEK OF REQUESTS.` → `NINETEEN BLESSINGS ON A WEEKDAY.` → `ON SHABBAT, THE MIDDLE IS GONE.`

segments.voice: On Shabbat, the Amidah keeps its first three blessings, the praise, and its last three, the thanks and the peace. But the thirteen requests in the middle are taken out. In their place goes a single blessing called kedushat hayom, the holiness of the day. So the Sabbath Amidah has seven blessings instead of nineteen. Why remove the requests? The Talmud's answer is short: out of honor for Shabbat, the rabbis didn't want to weigh people down. Later teachers add that asking for your needs means thinking about everything that's wrong, illness, debt, the harvest, and Shabbat isn't the day for that. The day isn't for fixing your life. It's for living it as if it were already enough. There's a striking line in the Talmud about visiting the sick on Shabbat. You don't pray at length for their recovery. Instead, the Talmud gives the words to say: it's Shabbat, we don't cry out; healing will come soon. The day itself is the comfort. That doesn't mean people stop caring on Shabbat, or stop hoping. Hearts still carry their worries in. The rabbis noticed that too, and some of their sources struggle with how much request is allowed. But the shape of the prayer makes a point. Six days a week you're a person with needs. One day a week, the prayer treats you as a person who has what they need. In it, a person comes before God not to ask, but just to be there. The middle blessing is the day itself.
screen: `NINETEEN BECOMES SEVEN.` · `ONE BLESSING: THE DAY'S HOLINESS.` · `NOT WEIGHED DOWN BY NEEDS.` · `HEALING WILL COME SOON.` · then, large: `NO REQUESTS TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go an hour without asking for anything. Start now, with the sit. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, don't ask for a single thing, not from God, not from yourself. No fix, no plan, no wish. When a request comes up, and it will, notice it, set it down beside you, and come back to the breath. Just be in what is. Then try to carry that for the next hour. The bell holds the time.
Kedushat hayom. The holiness of the day: the single blessing that replaces the weekday's thirteen requests on Shabbat.
Your line: already enough, just as it is. For one hour today, ask for nothing, and notice how often you want to. Day six hundred seventeen.

618.title: They shall keep it (Exodus 31:16–17)
618.hook: V'shamru is sung Friday night and Saturday morning
618.howItsDone: V'shamru (Exodus 31:16–17) is sung in the Friday evening service before the Amidah in many communities, said in the Shabbat morning Amidah in the Ashkenazi rite, and recited at the start of the daytime Kiddush in many homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shabbat Amidah, where nineteen blessings become seven. Your line was already enough, just as it is. How long did you last without asking? Today, two verses that turn up all over Shabbat. Day six hundred eighteen.

Some lines get stuck in a family. A grandparent's saying that comes out at every dinner. A song at every birthday. Two verses from Exodus are like that for Shabbat. They're sung on Friday night, right before the evening Amidah. They're said again inside the Saturday morning Amidah in many communities. And they open the Kiddush over wine at Saturday lunch in many homes. It's the kind of tune a child can hum before knowing what the words mean. It's called V'shamru, and they shall keep.
screen: `LINES STUCK IN A FAMILY.` → `FRIDAY NIGHT, SATURDAY MORNING, LUNCH.` → `V'SHAMRU: AND THEY SHALL KEEP.`

segments.voice: Here they are in the old Jewish translation, from Exodus thirty-one: "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between Me and the children of Israel for ever." Then the reason: because in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day ceased from work and rested. A few things are packed in there. First, keep. Shamar in Hebrew means to guard, to watch over, the way you'd keep a garden or keep a secret. Shabbat isn't only something you have. It's something you protect. Second, throughout their generations. Not a one-time event. A thing handed down, parent to child, like the tune. Third, a sign. Like a family name over a door: a small, visible thing that says there's a bond here. And then the last word of the passage, the one translated rested. In Hebrew it's vayinafash, built from nefesh, soul, or breath. Some render it was refreshed, or caught breath. The Talmud plays with that word. Resh Lakish taught that on Shabbat a person is given an extra soul, a neshamah yeteirah, and when Shabbat ends it's taken away. He read vayinafash as a play on words: vay, avdah nefesh. Alas, the soul is lost. Some readers hear in it a reason Saturday night can feel a little sad: something extra was there, and now it's going.
screen: `A SIGN FOR EVER.` · `SHAMAR: TO GUARD, TO KEEP.` · `THROUGHOUT THEIR GENERATIONS.` · `VAYINAFASH: AN EXTRA SOUL.` · then, large: `KEEP THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one line of it. If you know the tune, sing v'shamru, quietly. If not, take the English, and they shall keep, and sing it to any slow melody you like. Repeat it a few times. Then let the singing stop, and think of one hour this week you'd like to guard, the way you'd guard a garden gate. Breathe into that hour. The bell holds the time.
V'shamru. And they shall keep: Exodus 31's words for the Sabbath, a sign for ever, guarded and handed down, sung all through the day.
Your line: keep the sabbath. This week, mark off one hour and guard it: no work, no screens, just rest. Day six hundred eighteen.

619.title: Never enough thanks
619.hook: if our mouths were full of song as the sea, we still couldn't thank enough
619.carry: a mouth as full as the sea
619.howItsDone: Nishmat is said in the Shabbat and festival morning service after the Song at the Sea, and in many congregations the leader for the main part of the service begins near its end; it is also recited at the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, V'shamru, and the extra soul of Shabbat. Your line was keep the sabbath. Which hour did you guard? Today, Shabbat morning, and a thank-you that admits it can't finish. Day six hundred nineteen.

Have you ever tried to thank someone who saved you? A nurse who stayed through the night. A teacher who saw something in you. A stranger who pulled over in the rain. You open your mouth and the words are too small. Thank you sounds like what you'd say for passing the salt. Some debts are too big for language. On Shabbat and festival mornings, there's a prayer that starts from exactly that feeling, and doesn't try to hide it.
screen: `THANKING SOMEONE WHO SAVED YOU.` → `THE WORDS ARE TOO SMALL.` → `A PRAYER THAT ADMITS IT.`

segments.voice: It's called Nishmat, from its first words, nishmat kol chai: the breath of every living thing shall bless your name. It echoes the last line of the book of Psalms, in the old Jewish translation: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Hallelujah." Then comes its center. If our mouths were full of song as the sea, and our tongues full of joy like the roaring of its waves, and our lips full of praise like the wide sky, and our eyes shining like the sun and the moon, and our hands spread out like the eagles of heaven, and our feet as swift as deer, still we could not thank you enough for even one of the thousands upon thousands of kindnesses you have done for us and for our ancestors. Read it slowly and you notice what it's doing. It uses the whole body: mouth, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet. And it stretches each one to the size of the world: the sea, the sky, the sun. And then it admits defeat. That's the point. The thanks is in the admitting. Part of this language is old: the Talmud already quotes the line about mouths full of song as the sea, in a thanksgiving for rain. Nishmat is said on Shabbat and festival mornings, and it's also sung at the Passover seder, near the end. Many congregations mark it as a turning point in the Shabbat morning service: a new leader often steps up right around here. A thank-you that runs on and on, and then says it isn't long enough.
screen: `THE BREATH OF EVERY LIVING THING.` · `MOUTHS FULL OF SONG AS THE SEA.` · `THE WHOLE BODY, STRETCHED.` · `AND STILL NOT ENOUGH.` · then, large: `NEVER ENOUGH THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank beyond words. Settle, and breathe. Think of the one person, or the one gift, you could never thank enough. Try to say thank you for it, and notice how small the words are. Then stop using words. Let your breath be the thanks. Each breath in, the gift. Each breath out, the thanks you can't say. Let the breath of a living thing do it, as the prayer says. The bell holds the time.
Nishmat. The breath of. The Shabbat morning prayer that says even a mouth as full as the sea couldn't thank enough.
Your line: a mouth as full as the sea. Today, thank someone for something too big to thank them for, and tell them the words aren't enough. Day six hundred nineteen.

620.title: Seven are called
620.hook: on Shabbat morning seven people are called up to the Torah
620.howItsDone: On Shabbat morning the Torah portion is divided into at least seven aliyot, plus the maftir; each person called up recites a blessing before and after while a trained reader chants the section. Many congregations call a kohen first and a Levite second, and people are often honored at life events.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nishmat, thanks as wide as the sea and still not enough. Your line was a mouth as full as the sea. Who did you try to thank? Today, the Torah comes out on Shabbat morning, and people are called by name. Day six hundred twenty.
screen: `A MOUTH AS FULL AS THE SEA.`

segments.voice: A name is called out across the sanctuary. Someone stands up, a little surprised, and makes their way to the front. A teenager who just turned thirteen. A grandfather whose granddaughter was born this week. A woman about to be married, or a man who got out of the hospital on Tuesday. They step up to the open scroll, say a blessing, and stand there while a section is read. Then the next name is called. On Shabbat morning, this happens seven times.
screen: `A NAME IS CALLED.` → `UP TO THE OPEN SCROLL.` → `SEVEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: Being called up is an aliyah, a going up. Same word as moving to the Land of Israel. You rise to the Torah. The Mishnah, in tractate Megillah, sets the numbers, and they climb with the day. On Monday and Thursday mornings, and Shabbat afternoon: three people. On the new moon and the middle days of festivals: four. On festivals: five. On Yom Kippur: six. On Shabbat morning: seven. The more holy or restful the day, the more people get a turn. Then, after the seven, one more is called for a closing section, and that person reads the haftarah, the prophets' portion we met a few weeks ago. Who goes first? Traditionally a kohen, a descendant of the priests, then a Levite, then everyone else. The Mishnah gives the reason: for the sake of peace, so nobody fights over who goes first. Many congregations today keep that order. Some don't. And in many congregations women are called as well as men; in Orthodox congregations, men are called. Later authorities describe a change. Once, each person called up read their own section aloud. But not everyone could read the scroll, with no vowels and no punctuation. To spare people embarrassment, the custom became that a trained reader reads for everyone, and the person called up says the blessings and follows along. Seven people, one reader, a whole community in the passage. The portion is too big for one person to hold, so it's shared.
screen: `ALIYAH: GOING UP.` · `THREE, FOUR, FIVE, SIX, SEVEN.` · `KOHEN, LEVI, THEN EVERYONE.` · `ONE READER, SO NO ONE IS SHAMED.` · then, large: `SEVEN ARE CALLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see how many people take part. Settle, and breathe. Picture a gathering you belong to: a service, a family dinner, a team, a choir. Count, in your mind, how many people actually have a role in it. Who speaks, who serves, who carries, who cleans up. Then picture someone at the edges who could be called up next time. Hold their face for a while. The bell holds the time.
Aliyah. A going up: being called to read from the Torah, as on Shabbat morning, when seven people take their turn.
Your line: too big to hold alone. Today, invite one person into something you'd usually do alone or with the usual crowd. Day six hundred twenty.

621.title: The additional prayer
621.hook: an extra Amidah on Shabbat and festivals, for the extra Temple offering
621.howItsDone: Musaf is said after the Torah reading on Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh and the High Holy Days, as a silent Amidah with a repetition; Orthodox and Conservative congregations say it with different wording about the sacrifices, and many Reform congregations omit it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven people called up to the Torah. Your line was too big to hold alone. Who did you invite in? Today, the Torah goes back into the ark, and something extra begins. Day six hundred twenty-one.

On a weekday, the morning service winds down after the Amidah to a few closing prayers and Aleinu. On Shabbat, after the long Torah reading, just when you think it's over, everyone stands up again. Another silent Amidah. A whole extra prayer, at the end of a long morning. Visitors check how many pages are left. But this extra prayer is a mark of Shabbat and festival mornings. And to understand it, you have to go back to the Temple, and count the animals.
screen: `JUST WHEN YOU THINK IT'S OVER.` → `ANOTHER AMIDAH.` → `BACK TO THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Musaf means added, or additional. In the Temple, every day had two fixed offerings, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. The daily prayers stand in their place. But on Shabbat, the book of Numbers adds more: two more lambs, with flour and oil and wine, beyond the daily ones. Festivals and new moons got their own extra offerings too. So when the Temple was gone and prayer took the place of sacrifice, the extra day got an extra prayer. A verse from Hosea is often quoted for this whole idea. In the old Jewish translation: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Words instead of animals. What's inside Musaf? On Shabbat, the middle blessing names the day and recalls the extra offering from Numbers. And here's where Jewish movements differ, openly. Orthodox prayer books keep the hope for the Temple's offerings to be restored. Conservative prayer books keep Musaf but speak of the offerings as something our ancestors brought, in the past. Many Reform congregations leave Musaf out. Each is a way of answering the same question: what do we do with the memory of sacrifice? And on Rosh Hashanah, Musaf grows three great sections, on kingship, remembrance and the shofar. The kingship section opens with Aleinu, the prayer we met at the start of this stretch. Tradition says that was its first home. An extra day gets an extra portion, of words.
screen: `MUSAF: ADDED.` · `TWO MORE LAMBS ON SHABBAT.` · `THE OFFERING OF OUR LIPS.` · `MOVEMENTS ANSWER DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `AN EXTRA PORTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add one extra good thing today. Settle, and breathe. Look at what you were already going to do today: the ordinary offerings, so to speak. Work, meals, the drive, the dishes. Now choose one thing to add that wasn't required. A longer phone call. A walk. A note. A slower meal. Picture yourself doing it. Let it feel like an extra portion, given because the day deserves it. The bell holds the time.
Musaf. Additional. The extra Amidah of Shabbat, festivals and new moons, standing in for the extra Temple offering.
Your line: an extra portion. Today, do the one extra good thing you chose, and do it just because the day is worth it. Day six hundred twenty-one.

622.title: A taste of next week
622.hook: the Shabbat afternoon reading begins next week's portion
622.howItsDone: At Shabbat Mincha the Torah is taken out and three people are called up for the opening section of the next week's portion; the same section is read on Monday and Thursday mornings, before the full portion is read the following Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Musaf, the extra prayer for an extra day. Your line was an extra portion. What extra good thing did you add? Today, Shabbat afternoon, when the Torah comes out one more time. Day six hundred twenty-two.

TV shows end an episode with a few seconds of next week's story. Just enough so you come back. Shabbat afternoon has its own version. The morning's long reading is done, lunch has been eaten, maybe a nap was taken. Then, late in the day, at the afternoon service, the scroll comes out of the ark again. But it isn't rolled back to this week's portion. It's rolled forward. Three people are called up, and the congregation hears the opening of next week's portion. A preview.
screen: `A FEW SECONDS OF NEXT WEEK.` → `THE SCROLL COMES OUT AGAIN.` → `ROLLED FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Where does this come from? The Talmud, in tractate Bava Kamma, lists ten enactments it credits to Ezra the scribe, and reading the Torah at Shabbat afternoon prayer is one of them. The reason it gives is practical: for the shopkeepers. As the commentator Rashi explains, these were people too busy all week to hear Torah on Monday and Thursday. Wait, Monday and Thursday? Yes. That same short section, the opening of the coming week's portion, is read again on Monday and Thursday mornings. So the week has a rhythm. Saturday afternoon, a taste. Monday, again. Thursday, again. And then, next Saturday morning, the whole portion. The Talmud traces the Monday and Thursday readings to a verse from Exodus. Right after crossing the sea, the people "went three days in the wilderness, and found no water," and when they finally found some, it was bitter. The rabbis read water as Torah. Three days without it is too long. So the Torah is never more than three days away. In many communities, the afternoon service says a verse about timing just before the scroll comes out. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 69: "But as for me, let my prayer be unto Thee, O LORD, in an acceptable time." Late Shabbat afternoon is treated as one of those times. Notice what that does. Shabbat is about stopping, but it also leans forward. Even on the day of rest, you're handed a little of what's coming. You start next week before this week ends.
screen: `EZRA: FOR THE SHOPKEEPERS.` · `SATURDAY, MONDAY, THURSDAY.` · `NEVER THREE DAYS WITHOUT WATER.` · `IN AN ACCEPTABLE TIME.` · then, large: `A TASTE OF NEXT WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look ahead to next week's portion. If you can, find out its name and read its first few verses. If not, take a minute now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the week ahead, not as a list of tasks, but as a story about to begin. What's the first scene? What one thing are you looking forward to? Let yourself have a taste of it now, without worrying. The bell holds the time.
A taste of next week. The Shabbat afternoon reading, which opens the coming week's portion and comes back on Monday and Thursday.
screen: `A TASTE OF NEXT WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a taste of next week. Today, do one small thing that starts something you're looking forward to. Day six hundred twenty-two.

623.title: Afternoon learning
623.hook: summer Shabbat afternoons read Pirkei Avot; winter afternoons read psalms
623.howItsDone: Many communities study a chapter of Pirkei Avot each Shabbat afternoon from Passover to Shavuot, and many continue until Rosh Hashanah; in winter, Ashkenazi custom adds Psalm 104 and the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134) after the afternoon service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shabbat afternoon reading that previews next week. Your line was a taste of next week. What did you start? Today, what fills the rest of that long afternoon. Day six hundred twenty-three.

A summer Saturday, late. The light goes on forever. Lunch was hours ago, and there's still a long stretch before the stars come out and Shabbat ends. No phones, no errands, no work. What do you do with all that time? In some homes and synagogues, the answer is a small book of sayings, read one chapter a week. In winter, when the afternoons are short and dark, the answer changes to psalms. The calendar decides what you study.
screen: `A LONG SUMMER SATURDAY.` → `NO PHONES, NO ERRANDS.` → `THE CALENDAR DECIDES.`

segments.voice: The summer book is Pirkei Avot, the chapters of the fathers, a tractate of the Mishnah made almost entirely of sayings. It opens with a chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on, to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets, to the great assembly. Then the sages, one by one, each with a line or two. Hillel: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? Ben Zoma: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. Who is strong? The one who masters their own impulse. Who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion. The custom is to read one chapter each Shabbat afternoon, starting after Passover. Five chapters come from the Mishnah, and a sixth was added for this reading, so there's about one for each Shabbat between Passover and Shavuot. Some communities keep cycling through the summer until Rosh Hashanah. Then, in winter, Ashkenazi custom often turns to Psalm 104, which praises the whole created world. In the old Jewish translation: "How manifold are Thy works, O LORD!" And to the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, short songs pilgrims may have sung on the way up to Jerusalem. Why the switch? Customs differ in their reasons, and the sources don't settle it. But the pattern is clear. Long light, practical sayings about how to live. Short light, songs about the world and the climb. Either way, Shabbat afternoon isn't empty time. It's learning time.
screen: `PIRKEI AVOT: A CHAIN FROM SINAI.` · `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?` · `ONE CHAPTER EACH SHABBAT.` · `WINTER: PSALMS OF ASCENTS.` · then, large: `AFTERNOON LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one saying. Settle, and breathe. Take one of Ben Zoma's: who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion. Say it slowly, twice. Then look around you, at your portion right now. The room, the chair, the people in your life, your body breathing. Let the saying test it, gently. Is there enough here? Stay with the question, without hurrying to answer. The bell holds the time.
Afternoon learning. Pirkei Avot through the summer Shabbatot, and psalms through the winter ones.

Your line: if not now, when. A week of no requests, V'shamru, Nishmat, seven called, Musaf, a taste of next week and Avot. This afternoon, read one saying and carry it till evening. Day six hundred twenty-three.

pairs: who is rich? happy with their portion

myth: Pirkei Avot is a book of laws about prayer
it's a tractate of the Mishnah made almost entirely of sayings.
Avot is read one chapter at a time on Shabbat afternoons
starting after Passover, and in some places all summer.
the reason for reading psalms in winter is settled in the sources
customs give different reasons; the sources don't settle it.

fork.setup: Ben Zoma asks: who is rich? which answer does he give?
options: the one with the most land.
the one who is happy with their portion.
the one who gives the most away.
fork.reveal: the one who is happy with their portion. Avot chapter four.

original.note: Hebrew: chapters of the fathers, the Mishnah's book of sayings.
